extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, critics, and educated readers interested in wit and literary taste (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging and producing 'wit' in prose and poetry: distinguishing true wit from false devices (puns, anagrams, acrostics, etc.), with criteria, tests, and genre-appropriate advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Wit (resemblance of ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: True Wit consists in such a resemblance and congruity of ideas as gives Delight and Surprize to the Reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resemblance must not lie too near in the nature of things (obvious likeness gives no surprize). True wit appears where a congruity of ideas yields both delight and surprise; examples include well-turned metaphors and apt allusions (not merely verbal coincidences).

rubrics_metrics.name: False Wit (resemblance of words/letters/sounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: False Wit chiefly consists in the resemblance and congruity sometimes of single Letters (anagrams, chronograms, lipograms, acrosticks), sometimes of Syllables (echoes, doggerel rhymes), sometimes of Words (puns, quibbles), and sometimes of whole Sentences or Poems cast into shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices rely on form or sound rather than idea and are essentially superficial; they are described as 'vox et præterea nihil' (a sound, and nothing but a sound) and are to be regarded with scepticism as true wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixt Wit (part word, part idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixt Wit consists partly in the Resemblance of Ideas, and partly in the Resemblance of Words—a mixture of true and false wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This species appears often in poets like Cowley; its foundations are partly truth and partly extravagance. The essay advises that the proper province for mixt wit is epigram and short occasional pieces rather than sustained epic or heroic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Punning
rubrics_metrics.description: A Punn is a Conceit arising from the use of two Words that agree in the Sound, but differ in the Sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punning is a widespread, perennial device (Aristotle, Cicero examples). Historically common, it is nevertheless judged a form of false wit when it substitutes sound-play for meaningful resemblance of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for distinguishing true wit from puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate the expression into a different language; if it bears the test (survives translation), it may be pronounced true; if it vanishes, it is likely a pun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical test (recommended in the essay) distinguishes wit grounded in idea from mere phonetic coincidence: true wit should survive translation into another tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential qualities required of Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The two essential properties of Wit are Delight and Surprise (the latter more particularly essential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a resemblance to count as wit it must both please and surprise; mere aptness without surprise, or mere cleverness without delight, fails to be true wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance must be non-obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Resemblance of Ideas is not Wit, unless it be such an one that gives Delight and Surprise; where the Likeness is obvious, it gives no Surprize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing whiteness to snow without further novelty is not wit; adding an unexpected twist (e.g., 'and it is cold too') creates wit. Judges should seek that additional unexpected congruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of Words and Thoughts (Dryden's definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden's definition: Wit is 'a Propriety of Words and Thoughts adapted to the Subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay critiques this as too broad (would extend to all good writing), but recognizes propriety as an element: appropriate thought and diction matter though they do not alone constitute wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as the foundation of beautiful thought (Bouhours)
rubrics_metrics.description: No Thought can be beautiful which is not just; the Basis of all Wit is Truth—good Sense is the groundwork of valuable thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgment should favour thoughts grounded in truth and naturalness; ornament or verbal ingenuity without justness lacks real value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme and doggerel cannot redeem poor thought
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Thought of the Couplet in such Compositions is good, the Rhyme adds little to it; and if bad, it will not be in the Power of the Rhyme to recommend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhyme or clever sound-patterns should not be relied upon to elevate weak ideas; judges and writers should value thought over mere rhyming cleverness (doggerel often pleases ignorant readers but not true taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixt wit's appropriate genre: epigram
rubrics_metrics.description: The only Province for mixt Wit is Epigram, or those little occasional Poems that are a Tissue of Epigrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer, heroick, or serious forms should avoid mixt wit's reliance on verbal trickery; reserve it for short, pointed pieces where the blend of wordplay and idea can succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of fashionable but frivolous devices to avoid as serious wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices such as Anagrams, Acrosticks, Chronograms, Bouts-rimés, Lipograms, shaped poems, and artificial chronograms are cited as tricks of false wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms are described historically and ridiculed as labourious exercises that substitute artifice for real thought; the guidance is to treat them as curiosities rather than marks of genuine genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Wit and Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit lies in assemblage of ideas with quickness and variety; Judgment lies in separating carefully one from another to avoid being misled by resemblance or affinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that quick wit and clear judgment are different faculties: composition that chases novelty may lack sound judgment; critics should value both capacities where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/taste classification (Segrais)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers of poetry may be classed: the lowest ('Les Petits Esprits') prefer quibbles, conceits and epigrams rather than solid sense and elegant expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and judges should be aware of differing tastes: popularity with the 'mob' does not equate with true merit. Educative reading and exposure to better works can improve taste.
